title: Engineering drawings and its concepts
summary: Two things carry this subchapter. First, scale is a ratio of LIKE quantities, so 1:50 means one unit represents fifty of the same units — and a large-scale map has a large representative fraction and covers a small area in detail, which is the opposite of what the words suggest. Second, first angle projection puts the top view BELOW the front view, which is Indian and European practice; third angle puts it above. For sections, know which parts are never sectioned even when the cutting plane passes through them.

sections.heading: Drawing standards, lines and lettering
sections.body:
**Drawing sheet sizes** follow the **ISO A series**, each obtained by **halving the longer side** of the one before:

| Size | Dimensions (mm) |
|---|---|
| **A0** | **841 × 1189** (area **1 m²**) |
| A1 | 594 × 841 |
| A2 | 420 × 594 |
| A3 | 297 × 420 |
| **A4** | **210 × 297** |

**The whole series rests on the √2 ratio**: the sides are in the ratio **1 : √2**, which is the only ratio preserved when a rectangle is halved across its longer side. That is why an A1 drawing reduced to A2 keeps its proportions exactly, with no cropping or distortion — and why the whole system of sheet sizes, lettering heights and line thicknesses steps in the same ratio.

**Lettering heights (IS 9609)** step in the same progression:

> **2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm**

(each about √2 times the last), so a drawing reduced one sheet size still has legible lettering at the next standard height.

**Line types (IS 10714)** — the most examined item here:

| Line | Type | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous THICK** | ▬▬▬▬ | **Visible outlines and edges** |
| **Continuous THIN** | ──── | **Dimension lines, extension lines, leaders, HATCHING**, short centre lines |
| Continuous thin freehand or zig-zag | ∿∿∿ | **Short break** / long break lines |
| **Dashed (thin or medium)** | ─ ─ ─ | **HIDDEN edges and outlines** |
| **Chain THIN** (long dash short dash) | ─·─·─ | **CENTRE lines**, axes, pitch circles |
| **Chain thin, THICK at ends and changes of direction** | ▬·─·▬ | **CUTTING PLANE** |
| Chain thick | ▬·▬·▬ | Surfaces requiring special treatment |
| Chain thin double-dashed | ─··─·· | Adjacent parts, alternative positions, outline of the original before forming |

**Line thickness ratio** is **1 : 2** between thin and thick, chosen from the standard range **0.13, 0.18, 0.25, 0.35, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.4, 2.0 mm** — again a √2 progression.

**Precedence of lines** where two coincide, in order: **visible outline** > **hidden line** > **centre line**. So a hidden line is drawn in preference to a centre line at the same position, and a visible outline in preference to both.

**Dimensioning principles (IS 11669):**

| Principle | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Each dimension appears ONCE** | No duplication between views |
| Dimensions on the **view that shows the feature most clearly** | — |
| **Outside the outline** wherever possible | Keeps the view uncluttered |
| **Smaller dimensions nearer the view**, larger further out | Avoids crossing dimension and extension lines |
| **Units** stated once (usually mm) in the title block | Not repeated on each dimension |
| **Aligned or unidirectional** system, used consistently | Aligned: figures parallel to the dimension line, read from the bottom or right. Unidirectional: all figures horizontal |
| **Never dimension to a hidden line** | Use a section instead |

The last rule matters: a dimension to a hidden edge is ambiguous, because the reader cannot see exactly what is being measured. If a feature needs dimensioning and is hidden, the correct response is to **draw a section** that reveals it.

**The title block** carries: the **title**, **scale**, **drawing number**, **units**, **projection symbol**, **date**, and the names of the **drawn by, checked by and approved by** persons. The **projection symbol** — a truncated cone drawn in first or third angle — tells the reader which convention has been used, and its presence is not optional.

sections.heading: Scales
sections.body:
**A scale is a RATIO OF LIKE QUANTITIES**, and therefore **dimensionless**:

> **Representative fraction RF = drawing size / actual size**

So **1:50** means **one unit on the drawing represents fifty of the SAME units on the object** — 1 mm represents 50 mm, 1 cm represents 50 cm. A statement that "1 mm represents 50 cm" is a scale of **1:500**, not 1:50, and it is the standard distractor.

| RF | Type | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **RF < 1** | **REDUCING** | **Maps, buildings, site plans** — the object is larger than the paper |
| RF = 1 | **Full size** | Ordinary machine drawings |
| **RF > 1** | **ENLARGING** | Small components — a watch part, a bolt thread |

**Recommended scales (IS 10713)** follow a decimal-and-halving progression, so they are convenient to read off and consistent between drawings:

> **Reducing: 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200, 1:500, 1:1000**
> **Enlarging: 2:1, 5:1, 10:1**

**Typical civil engineering scales:**

| Drawing | Scale |
|---|---|
| **Location / key plan** | 1:5000 – 1:50 000 |
| **Site plan** | **1:500 – 1:1000** |
| **Building plans, sections, elevations** | **1:50 – 1:100** |
| **Detail drawings** (joints, reinforcement) | **1:5 – 1:20** |
| Road longitudinal section | 1:1000 horizontal, **1:100 vertical** (exaggerated) |
| Road cross-section | 1:100 |
| **Topographic map** | **1:25 000 – 1:250 000** |
| Cadastral plan | 1:500 – 1:5000 |

**Exaggerated vertical scale** on a longitudinal section is worth noting: a road's vertical change over a kilometre is a few metres, so plotting both axes at the same scale would produce a nearly flat line in which nothing could be read. **Exaggerating the vertical scale ten times** makes the gradients visible — at the cost that the section looks far steeper than reality, which must be remembered when interpreting it.

**The large-scale / small-scale terminology trap:**

> A **LARGE-scale map has a LARGE representative fraction** (e.g. **1:500**) and covers a **SMALL area in GREAT detail**.
> A **SMALL-scale map has a SMALL RF** (e.g. **1:1 000 000**) and covers a **LARGE area with LITTLE detail**.

**The words describe the fraction, not the area** — and since 1/500 is a much larger number than 1/1 000 000, the naming is consistent even though it seems backward. This is a favourite question.

**Types of scale drawn on a sheet:**

| Scale | Reads to |
|---|---|
| **Plain scale** | Two units — metres and decimetres |
| **Diagonal scale** | **Three** units — metres, decimetres and centimetres |
| **Vernier scale** | Three units, more precisely |
| **Comparative scale** | Two different unit systems on one scale |
| Scale of chords | Angles |

**Why a GRAPHICAL scale bar is drawn on the sheet** is the practical point:

> Paper **shrinks and stretches** with humidity, and drawings are **photocopied, scanned and reduced**. The **stated ratio then no longer holds** — but a **scale bar drawn on the sheet scales with the reproduction** and remains correct.

That is why every map and site plan carries one, and why a dimension **scaled from a drawing** is never as reliable as a **figured dimension**. The convention "**do not scale from this drawing**" printed on construction drawings exists for exactly this reason: if a dimension is needed, it should be **written**, and if it is missing the drawing should be queried rather than measured.

sections.heading: Projection
sections.body:
**Orthographic projection** represents a three-dimensional object by **two-dimensional views on mutually perpendicular planes**, the projectors being **parallel and perpendicular to the plane**.

**The three principal planes and their views:**

| Plane | View |
|---|---|
| **Vertical plane (VP)** | **Front view (elevation)** |
| **Horizontal plane (HP)** | **Top view (plan)** |
| **Profile plane (PP)** | **Side view (end elevation)** |

**First angle and third angle projection — the distinction examined every sitting:**

| | **FIRST angle** | **THIRD angle** |
|---|---|---|
| Object is placed | **Between the observer and the plane** | The **plane is between the observer and the object** |
| **Top view is placed** | **BELOW the front view** | **ABOVE the front view** |
| **Left side view is placed** | **on the RIGHT** of the front view | on the **LEFT** |
| Used in | **India, Nepal, Europe** (the IS standard) | **USA, Canada, Australia** |
| Symbol | A truncated cone with the **small end on the left** | Small end on the **right** |

**The mnemonic for first angle**: the object is **between the observer and the plane**, so each view is **pushed through the object to the FAR side** — the observer looks from above, the view appears below. In third angle the plane is between, so the view appears on the **near** side, like looking into a glass box.

**A drawing must state which convention it uses**, by the **projection symbol in the title block**. Reading a first-angle drawing as third-angle produces a **mirror-image misinterpretation** — a genuine and expensive error, and the reason the symbol is mandatory.

**The second and fourth angles are not used**, because in them the views would **overlap** when the planes are rotated into one plane.

**Number of views.** The minimum number that **fully describes the object without ambiguity** — usually **three** (front, top, side), sometimes **two** for a simple object, and more for a complex one. **Redundant views should be omitted**; every view costs drawing and checking effort and can introduce inconsistency.

**Choosing the front view** is the first decision: it should be the view that **shows the most characteristic shape** and the **fewest hidden lines**, and it should represent the object in its **natural or functional position**.

**Auxiliary views** are projected onto a plane **inclined to the principal planes**, used to show the **true shape of an inclined face**. A face inclined to all three principal planes appears **foreshortened** in every ordinary view, so its true shape and true dimensions can only be shown by an auxiliary view — which is exactly when one is drawn.

**Pictorial projections** show three dimensions in one view:

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Isometric** | Three axes at **120°** to each other; all axes **equally foreshortened** (isometric scale ≈ **0.816** of true length, though a full-size isometric drawing is usually drawn) |
| Dimetric | Two axes equally foreshortened |
| Trimetric | All three differently |
| **Oblique (cavalier, cabinet)** | The front face is drawn **true shape**, with the depth at an angle (45° usual); **cabinet** halves the depth |
| **Perspective** | Converging projectors — the most realistic, used for **architectural presentation** |

**Isometric is the engineering pictorial** because the three axes are equally treated and **measurements can be taken along them**, which is not true of perspective. **Perspective is the architectural pictorial** because it shows the object as the eye sees it — but it cannot be measured, which is why it is used for presentation and never for construction.

**Development of surfaces** — unrolling a surface into a plane — is used for sheet metal work, ducts, hoppers and transitions. **Parallel line development** for prisms and cylinders, **radial line development** for pyramids and cones, and **triangulation** for transition pieces. **A sphere cannot be developed exactly** — which is why a spherical tank is fabricated from approximated segments and why every flat map of the earth distorts something.

sections.heading: Sections and civil engineering drawings
sections.body:
**A sectional view** shows the object as if **cut through**, so that internal features appear as **visible outlines** rather than a confusion of hidden dashed lines.

**Conventions (IS 10714 and IS 11669):**

| Convention | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Hatching (section lining)** | **Thin continuous lines at 45°** to the principal outline |
| **Adjacent parts** | Hatched at **different angles or spacings**, so the parts are distinguishable |
| **The same part in different views** | Hatched **identically** throughout |
| **Large areas** | Hatching may be limited to a **band along the outline** |
| **Very thin sections** (gaskets, sheet, structural steel in a small-scale view) | May be shown **SOLID BLACK** |
| **Hidden lines** | **OMITTED** in the sectioned portion — they are now visible |
| Adjacent thin sections | Separated by a small gap |

**The cutting plane** is shown on an **adjacent view** by a **thin chain line, thickened at its ends and at every change of direction**, with **arrows** giving the direction of viewing and **capital letters** identifying the section (A–A, B–B).

**Parts that are NOT sectioned** even when the cutting plane passes through them — the most examined item:

> **Shafts, bolts, nuts, screws, rivets, keys, pins, cotters, ribs, webs, spokes, gear teeth, and rolling elements (balls, rollers)**

**Why.** For **fasteners and shafts**, sectioning adds no information — they are solid and their construction is known — and it makes the drawing harder to read. For **ribs and webs**, the reason is different and more important: **hatching them would give a false impression of solidity**, suggesting a thick mass of material where in fact there is a thin plate. A rib sectioned longitudinally would appear identical to a solid boss, which is precisely the misreading the convention prevents.

**Types of section:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Full section** | The cutting plane passes **right through** |
| **Half section** | **Half sectioned, half external** — shows both internal and external form in one view; used for **symmetrical** objects |
| **Offset section** | The cutting plane is **stepped**, to pass through several features not in one plane |
| **Revolved section** | A local cross-section **rotated into place** on the view |
| **Removed section** | The same, but **placed elsewhere** on the sheet |
| **Broken-out (partial) section** | A **small area only**, bounded by a **break line** |
| Aligned section | Features rotated into the plane of the section (e.g. spokes of a wheel) |

**The half section is the elegant one**: for a symmetrical object it conveys the internal and external form **in a single view**, with the sectioned half normally placed to the **right** or **below** the centre line, and **no hidden lines shown** in either half.

**Civil engineering drawings and their conventions:**

| Drawing | Shows |
|---|---|
| **Site / location plan** | The plot, boundaries, access, orientation, existing features |
| **Layout plan** | The building or structure on the site |
| **Floor plan** | A **horizontal section at about 1 m above floor level**, looking down |
| **Elevation** | The external face, as seen from one direction |
| **SECTION** | A vertical cut — **where the real construction information is** |
| **Detail drawings** | Junctions, reinforcement, joints, at large scale |
| **Working / construction drawings** | Fully dimensioned, for building from |
| **As-built drawings** | Recording what was **actually** constructed |

**A floor plan IS a section** — a horizontal one, cut at about 1 m so that doors, windows and sills are cut through and appear in the plan. That is why window and door openings are shown with their sills and lintels, and it is a point candidates rarely notice.

**Why the SECTION is the most important civil drawing:**

> A building or a structure is understood chiefly through its **SECTIONS**, because that is where the information a contractor actually needs is conveyed. A **plan shows layout**; a **section shows construction**.

| Section | Conveys |
|---|---|
| **Wall section** | Foundation, plinth, **DPC**, wall construction, floor and roof junctions, finishes — the whole vertical assembly |
| **Beam or column section** | **Reinforcement layout**, bar sizes, cover, links |
| **Road cross-section** | **Camber**, carriageway, shoulders, side drains, cut and fill slopes, pavement layers |
| Canal or drain section | Bed, side slopes, lining, free board |
| Dam section | Zones, core, filters, drainage |

**Structural drawings** have their own conventions:

| Drawing | Content |
|---|---|
| **General arrangement (GA)** | Layout, member sizes, levels, grid references |
| **Reinforcement detail drawing** | Bar marks, sizes, spacing, shapes, cover — with a **bar bending schedule** |
| **Bar bending schedule** | Bar mark, diameter, shape with dimensions, **cutting length**, number, weight |
| Formwork / shuttering drawing | For the temporary works |

**Reinforcement drawing conventions**: bars are shown as **single thick lines** (not to their true thickness), each with a **bar mark** identifying it in the schedule, and a **section** is provided at every change of arrangement. The **cover** must be stated, since it is invisible in the finished work and determines the durability.

**Grid lines and levels:**

| Convention | Note |
|---|---|
| **Grid lines** | Lettered one way (A, B, C) and numbered the other (1, 2, 3); columns located by grid reference |
| **Levels** | Given as **reduced levels** relative to a stated **datum**, marked with a level symbol |
| **North point** | On every plan |
| **Section marks** | Referencing the section drawing |

**CAD and BIM.** Drawings are now produced in **CAD**, and increasingly as **BIM (Building Information Modelling)** — a three-dimensional model carrying **data** as well as geometry, from which drawings, quantities and schedules are extracted automatically. Its advantage over CAD is **consistency**: a change made once propagates to every drawing and schedule, eliminating the classic error of a detail revised on one drawing and not another. Its requirement is a discipline of modelling correctly at the outset, and a shared standard among the design team.

formulas.label: Representative fraction
formulas.expression: RF = drawing size / actual size     (a ratio of LIKE quantities, dimensionless)
formulas.note: 1:50 means one unit represents fifty of the SAME units. RF < 1 reducing, = 1 full size, > 1 enlarging.

formulas.label: Large-scale versus small-scale map
formulas.expression: LARGE scale = LARGE RF (1:500) = SMALL area in GREAT detail. SMALL scale = small RF (1:1 000 000) = large area, little detail.
formulas.note: The words describe the FRACTION, not the area — which is why the naming seems backward.

formulas.label: Sheet sizes and the √2 ratio
formulas.expression: A0 = 841 × 1189 mm (1 m²); each size halves the longer side. Sides in the ratio 1 : √2.
formulas.note: Lettering heights (2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm) and line thicknesses step in the same ratio.

formulas.label: First and third angle projection
formulas.expression: FIRST angle: top view BELOW the front view (India, Nepal, Europe). THIRD angle: top view ABOVE (USA).
formulas.note: In first angle the object is between the observer and the plane, so views are pushed to the FAR side.

formulas.label: Precedence of lines
formulas.expression: visible outline > hidden line > centre line

formulas.label: Parts never sectioned
formulas.expression: shafts, bolts, nuts, screws, rivets, keys, pins, RIBS, WEBS, spokes, gear teeth, rolling elements
formulas.note: Ribs and webs are excluded because hatching would falsely suggest a solid mass where there is a thin plate.

formulas.label: Hatching conventions
formulas.expression: thin continuous lines at 45°; adjacent parts at different angles; the same part identically in all views; very thin sections solid black
formulas.note: Hidden lines are OMITTED in the sectioned portion — they are now visible.

formulas.label: Isometric projection
formulas.expression: Three axes at 120°, equally foreshortened; isometric scale ≈ 0.816 of true length
formulas.note: Isometric can be measured along its axes; perspective cannot, which is why perspective is for presentation only.
